title: The Curtain and the Sierras: la joyita argentina, the Canaro Years, and Sixty Years of Silence
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ituzaingó, the birth on the flat land
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es.wikipedia. The coordinate is modern Ituzaingó and not the estancia, which is named Los Paraísos in one lens of the research pool and is not geolocated in any source reached here. The paternity is reported by es.wikipedia and is disputed in the literature; it is recorded, not adjudicated.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of August a daughter is born on the flat land west of Buenos Aires and registered as Aída Elsa Ada Falcone. Her mother is Cornelia Boesio. Her father is given as the landowner Miguel Nazar Anchorena, said to have died of cancer in France before the birth; the paternity is disputed in the literature and the register is the whole of the evidence. Two older sisters, Amanda and Adhelma, sing as well. Neither of them will be heard past the provinces.
suggested_refs: The birth registration of Aída Elsa Ada Falcone at Ituzaingó, Buenos Aires province, August 1905

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the letter taken off the name
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia states that at the age of four she told her mother she wished to sing, and that her mother shortened Falcone to Falcón. The year 1909 is arithmetic from her age and is not in the source; month and day default to 01. The pin is the corpus's generic Buenos Aires coordinate, no family address being attested.
stops.campa: At four she tells her mother she wants to sing. Cornelia Boesio does not treat this as a child's remark. She takes over the girl's career herself and takes a letter off the end of the surname: Falcone becomes Falcón, shorter on a bill, closing on the stress. The two of them will go on sharing a room for another seventy-two years, the last thirty-nine of those in a small house in the sierras of Córdoba. From this year the mother is manager and chaperone. The daughter is four years old and has a stage name.
suggested_refs: The stage name Falcón, contracted from the family surname Falcone by Cornelia Boesio

stops.name: Sociedad de San Vicente de Paúl, the debut of la joyita argentina
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia states she debuted as la joyita argentina at an event of the Sociedad de San Vicente de Paul and gives no year, no venue, and no programme. The date here orders the segment only. One lens of the research pool credited this to a todotango biography; that attribution is wrong, the URL used resolving to an unrelated singer, and the claim rests on es.wikipedia alone. The generic Buenos Aires pin replaces an unanchored placeholder coordinate.
stops.campa: She is put on at a charity function of the Sociedad de San Vicente de Paúl and billed as la joyita argentina, the little Argentine jewel. The name outlasts everything she earns later: a hundred and three years on, the museum made out of her house in Córdoba will still be called La Joyita. A room full of adults pays attention to a very small girl. Nobody writes down the address of the hall, or the date, or what she sang, and the Sociedad's programmes for these years were not located in this research.
suggested_refs: The charity programmes of the Sociedad de San Vicente de Paúl in Buenos Aires, c. 1909-1910, not located in this research

stops.name: Teatro Apolo, the tonadillas on Corrientes
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia places the Apolo tonadillas immediately before the 1919 film and gives no year; the figure 1916 that circulates comes from back-computing en.wikipedia's statement that she started in the theatre at eleven. The two encyclopedias are not reconciled here. The coordinate is the Apolo's site at Corrientes 1372, correcting a pin about 350 metres to the northeast.
stops.campa: On Corrientes, at the Apolo, she sings tonadillas, the Spanish comic songs a child could carry and an audience would forgive. It is a working stage, not a recital room, and she is a paid turn between other turns. Spanish Wikipedia sets this just before her first film; English Wikipedia says she began in the theatre at eleven. The two do not agree on the year and neither of them names a night. She is somewhere between eleven and thirteen years old.
suggested_refs: The Teatro Apolo, Corrientes 1372, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El festín de los caranchos
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia gives 1919 and en.wikipedia gives 1918; the disagreement is flagged and not resolved. Month and day default to 01. No shooting location is named in either source, so the generic Buenos Aires pin is used.
stops.campa: She appears in El festín de los caranchos, a silent picture, at about fourteen. There is no sound in it, which means the one thing she is good at is not in it either; she is there as a face. Argentine cinema at this date is a few men with cameras and borrowed money, and the film survives now mainly as a title inside her own biography. Her next screen appearance will be fifteen years off, and by then the pictures will talk. Spanish Wikipedia dates the picture 1919, English Wikipedia dates it 1918, and neither cites the other.
suggested_refs: El festín de los caranchos, silent film, Buenos Aires, 1918 or 1919

segments.name: The Third Woman to Make a Record

stops.name: RCA Victor, the first sides with Fresedo
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es.wikipedia, which states she began work with the RCA Victor recording room on 15 July 1925 accompanied by Osvaldo Fresedo's orchestra, and calls her the third Argentine woman to record a disc, not specifically the third to record tango. The studio address is not named in any source reached, so the generic Buenos Aires pin is used.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of July she begins work in the recording room of RCA Victor, with Osvaldo Fresedo's orchestra behind her. Rosita Quiroga and Azucena Maizani had gone first, in 1923; she is the third Argentine woman to put her voice on a disc. The machine rewards a particular kind of singer, one who can hold a line without a hall to carry it, and she can hold one. Seventeen years of continuous studio work start here, in a room with a horn in it. She is nineteen years old.
suggested_refs: The RCA Victor Buenos Aires recording ledgers for July 1925, not reached in this research

stops.name: Odeón, fourteen sides with Delfino and Parada
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the fourteen pieces, the label Odeón, Enrique Delfino at the piano and Manuel Parada on guitar, and the mezzo-soprano register, but gives no date within 1929; month and day default to 01. The studio address is not named. The sequence relative to the Canaro contract of 24 July is inferred from the sources' own ordering.
stops.campa: She comes back to the studios for Odeón and cuts fourteen pieces with Enrique Delfino at the piano and Manuel Parada on guitar, an accompaniment small enough to leave the voice with nowhere to hide. What people notice is the register. She is a mezzo-soprano among tango singers who mostly sing high and bright, and the low covered sound does something to the repertoire that nobody has heard done to it before. Six months later she is standing in front of Francisco Canaro's orchestra.
suggested_refs: The fourteen Odeón sides of 1929 with Enrique Delfino and Manuel Parada; no reissue history could be established in this research

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La morocha and the Canaro contract
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es.wikipedia, which states the working relationship with Francisco Canaro began on 24 July 1929 with the recording of the tango La morocha, and gives roughly 180 pieces recorded together. The label for this session is not named by the source; the Odeón attribution that circulates is an inference and is not carried here. The authorship of La morocha is attested separately by es.wikipedia's article on the song.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of July she begins her working relationship with Francisco Canaro's orchestra, and they open it with La morocha: Enrique Saborido's melody and Ángel Villoldo's words, a dark-haired criolla introducing herself and proud of it, written a quarter-century earlier on a wager in a bar before dawn. The oldest thing in the room is the song. Neither of them will ever say in public what else the arrangement was. Over the next nine years they will put something like a hundred and eighty sides on record.
suggested_refs: La morocha, music by Enrique Saborido and lyrics by Ángel Villoldo, first published 1905
sources: TodoTango, biography of Ada Falcón, reached only in cached summary

stops.name: Mendoza, the vals for a murdered governor
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the romance with Carlos Washington Lencinas, its end with his assassination in November 1929, and the vals Sueño con él composed in his memory; es.wikipedia's article on Lencinas fixes the killing to 10 November 1929 in Mendoza. One lens of the research pool tagged this romance as unverified tradition; that tag was wrong and is corrected here. Whether she was ever physically in Mendoza is not stated by any source reached.
stops.campa: Her lover is Carlos Washington Lencinas, former governor of Mendoza, caudillo of the wine province and open enemy of Hipólito Yrigoyen's government. In November he is shot dead. She writes a vals for him, Sueño con él, I dream of him, and that is the whole public record of the affair: a title and a grave in Mendoza. She is twenty-four, and four months later she is back at the microphone on schedule. Whether she ever set foot in Mendoza, at the burial or after, no source reached here says.
suggested_refs: The vals Sueño con él, composed by Ada Falcón in memory of Carlos Washington Lencinas

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the radio circuit
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia lists the stations Radio Cultura, Stentor, Splendid, Argentina, Prieto, Belgrano and El Mundo and says she debuted on them, not that she performed regularly on each; the fifteen discs a month and the 1930s framing are its own. The two hundred songs and the 1930-1942 peak come from en.wikipedia. The stations are collapsed into one stop because four of them carried an identical placeholder coordinate in the research pool, which was positively wrong for Radio Belgrano.
stops.campa: She debuts on Radio Cultura, then Stentor, Splendid, Argentina, Prieto, Belgrano, El Mundo. Seven stations, and the voice is in kitchens and shops all over the country at hours when nobody has bought a ticket for anything. She is cutting something like fifteen discs a month. Broadcasting in Argentina is barely ten years old and she is among the first people it makes national rather than merely famous in a city. She is twenty-five. Between 1930 and 1942 she will record roughly two hundred songs.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires broadcasting stations of the early 1930s: Cultura, Stentor, Splendid, Argentina, Prieto, Belgrano, El Mundo

stops.name: Palermo Chico, the house of three floors
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia and en.wikipedia both attest the three-storey house in Palermo Chico, the furs and jewellery and the two automobiles, and its sale in 1942; no purchase date is given anywhere, so this date orders the segment only. The coordinate is the corpus's existing Palermo Chico pin, which differs from the one in the research pool by about a kilometre. The Discépolo line is a two-layer attribution, his words inside her own 1995 recollection.
stops.campa: She lives in Palermo Chico, in a house of three floors, with furs, jewellery, and two automobiles at the kerb. It is the quarter of embassies and curved streets, laid out for people who are not asked to explain their money, and she has bought into it on royalties from tangos about people who have none. No source reached names the street, and no source names anybody living in the house except her mother. Enrique Santos Discépolo, who wrote some of those tangos, says of her that she is so divine it does you harm to look at her.
stops.quote: Es tan divina, que hace mal mirarla.
stops.quote_source: Enrique Santos Discépolo on Ada Falcón, recalled by her in a 1995 interview and quoted in Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002
suggested_refs: The three-storey Falcón house in Palermo Chico (Barrio Parque), sold 1942, street address unestablished
sources: Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the vals about her eyes
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests that Canaro composed the vals Yo no sé qué me han hecho tus ojos inspired by her eyes and dates it 1933; month and day default to 01. The quote is her own recollection given to Clarín in 1995 and printed in the 5 January 2002 obituary, sixty-two years after the vals; it is verbatim and is not contemporary with this stop.
stops.campa: Canaro writes a vals about her eyes and calls it Yo no sé qué me han hecho tus ojos, I don't know what your eyes have done to me. It becomes one of the most recorded pieces in the language and it is also, in the plainest reading, a declaration made in public by a married man about a woman standing inside his own orchestra. Everyone hears it and nobody says anything, and Canaro stays married. Sixty-two years afterwards a reporter asks her what she had looked like.
stops.quote: ¡Qué ojos! Usted no se imagina lo que era yo. Bastaba con mirarme los hoyitos de las mejillas, los dientes, las piernas.
stops.quote_source: Ada Falcón, recalling to Clarín in 1995, quoted in Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002
suggested_refs: The vals Yo no sé qué me han hecho tus ojos, by Francisco Canaro, 1933
sources: Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ídolos de la radio
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the film, the director Eduardo Morera, and the cast including Ignacio Corsini, Olinda Bozán, Dorita Davis and Tita Merello; no release date within 1934 is given, and month and day default to 01. No shooting location is named, so the generic Buenos Aires pin is used rather than a second invented studio coordinate.
stops.campa: Eduardo Morera directs Ídolos de la radio and casts the voices the country already knows: Ignacio Corsini, Olinda Bozán, Dorita Davis, Tita Merello, and Falcón, who is twenty-nine. Sound has arrived in Argentine cinema and the industry's first instinct is to photograph the radio, putting five people already in every house in the country on a screen so that the country can finally match the faces to the voices it knows. Her own face is in it for the length of a picture and then never again. It is the second film she makes and the last.
suggested_refs: Ídolos de la radio, directed by Eduardo Morera, Buenos Aires, 1934

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the decision to stop being seen
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates to 1935 her decision to make no further public appearances, describing her as then in her greatest period of splendour; month and day default to 01. No cause is given by the source and none is supplied here.
stops.campa: At the highest point of her career she decides she will make no more public appearances. It is not a retirement. She goes on recording, goes on broadcasting, goes on being the most heard woman in Argentina; what stops is the part where people can look at her. From this year the country hears Ada Falcón constantly and sees her almost never. No illness is named, no contract dispute, no quarrel with anyone: the source gives the year and no cause at all.
suggested_refs: The 1935 withdrawal from public performance, recorded without stated cause in es.wikipedia

stops.name: Radio El Mundo, the small room called sala Falcón
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia states that Radio El Mundo put at her disposal the sala F, of smaller dimensions, which people called la sala Falcón; it gives no date. es.wikipedia's article on Radio El Mundo dates the station's first broadcast to 29 November 1935, so the assignment cannot precede December 1935 and is dated here to 1936. The coordinate is the station's Maipú 555 building, correcting a pin about 300 metres to the northwest. The room is la sala F, not an officially named Sala Falcón.
stops.campa: Radio El Mundo opens on Maipú at the end of 1935, the most modern station in South America, and gives her a room of her own: sala F, the small one, which everybody in the building starts calling la sala Falcón. It is a courtesy and it is also a boundary drawn into a floor plan. The source names the room and not the year, and the room is sala F, never an officially titled Sala Falcón. She sings into a microphone in a space about the size of an office, and the signal goes out over the whole republic.
suggested_refs: The Radio El Mundo building at Maipú 555, Buenos Aires, and its studio F

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the pistol at the rehearsal
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The story of Canaro's wife bursting into a rehearsal with a pistol circulates widely in secondary press accounts and no contemporary account of it was located in this research; the venue is unknown and the generic Buenos Aires pin is a placeholder. Only the September 1938 end of the partnership is documented. The stop is kept because the legend is part of the record of what was said about her, and it is marked as legend.
stops.campa: The story everyone tells: Canaro's wife walks into a rehearsal, finds Falcón in his arms, and produces a pistol. It is repeated in the press for sixty years and no contemporary account of it has been found. The pistol may be somebody's invention; no telling of it names the hall. What is documented is the arithmetic underneath it: a divorce would have cost Canaro the orchestra, the catalogue and the money, he never left his wife, and the partnership ends in September of this year.
suggested_refs: The pistol anecdote as it circulates in the Argentine press; no primary contemporary account located
sources: Secondary press tradition, unlocated in primary form
Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Ada Falcón', for the dated end of the partnership

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the end of the Canaro years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es.wikipedia. No statement by either party about the cause was located in this research. The count of roughly 180 recordings is es.wikipedia's.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of September the working relationship with Francisco Canaro ends. Nine years, roughly a hundred and eighty recordings, and not a word of explanation from either side. She is thirty-three. She goes on recording for four more years; he keeps the orchestra, the catalogue, and the marriage. Neither of them is ever quoted on the date, on the reason, or on each other. The date is attested to the day; the cause is not attested anywhere at all.
suggested_refs: The Canaro-Falcón discography, roughly 180 sides, 1929-1938; no reissue history could be established here

stops.name: Radio El Mundo, singing to a cloth
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia gives 'hacia 1940', toward 1940, for her singing from behind a curtain hidden from her own musicians; month and day default to 01. One lens of the research pool dated this to 1939, which contradicts the source and is corrected here. The station is not named by the source for this detail; Radio El Mundo is inferred from the sala F arrangement and the pin is used accordingly.
stops.campa: Toward 1940 she is singing from behind a hung curtain, hidden not from an audience, since there is no audience, but from the musicians accompanying her. The orchestra plays to a cloth. She is thirty-four years old, at the top of her profession, and has arranged her working life so that nobody in the building can see her face. Whatever this is, the sources do not diagnose it. Spanish Wikipedia gives it one sentence and moves on to the next year, and no memoir by any of the musicians standing on the other side of the cloth was found.
suggested_refs: The curtained broadcasts of c. 1940, recorded in a single sentence of es.wikipedia

stops.name: Nueva Pompeya, the basilica on Avenida Sáenz
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the devotion, naming the church of Pompeya specifically and stating that her active religious life there gave rise to the rumours; it gives no dates and no frequency, so this date orders the segment only. What the source does not support, and what is not claimed here, is that contemporaries read the devotion as a sign of what was coming. The coordinate is the basilica on Avenida Sáenz, correcting a pin about 1.2 kilometres to the west.
stops.campa: In the south of the city, on Avenida Sáenz, the Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Rosario de Pompeya stands in a barrio of tanneries and the meat trade, about as far from Palermo Chico as the map allows. Out of her devotion there comes the rumour that the singer has secretly become a nun; she is not a nun, and she corrects nobody. She is at the church often enough that people notice, and the encyclopedia that records the devotion names this one and no other.
suggested_refs: The Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Rosario de Pompeya, Avenida Sáenz, Nueva Pompeya, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the last two sides
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the two final recordings, the tango Corazón encadenado and the vals Viviré con tu recuerdo, both by Canaro and Ivo Pelay, and dates them to 1942 without month or day; the defaults are 01. The claim circulating elsewhere that Ignacio Corsini duetted on Corazón encadenado was not confirmed in any source reached and is not carried here.
stops.campa: The last records she makes are a tango, Corazón encadenado, and a vals, Viviré con tu recuerdo, both written by Canaro with Ivo Pelay. She is thirty-six. Nobody staged this and nobody knew it was the end of anything; it is simply what the studio had scheduled. She sings them, the wax is cut, and the voice that has been in every house in Argentina for seventeen years does not enter a recording room again. Viviré con tu recuerdo: I will live with your memory.
suggested_refs: Corazón encadenado and Viviré con tu recuerdo, music by Francisco Canaro, words by Ivo Pelay, recorded 1942

stops.name: Palermo Chico, the house sold and the rest given away
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia and en.wikipedia attest the sale of the house and two automobiles and the distribution of her possessions to friends in 1942; no month is given and June is chosen only to place the sale after the last recordings and before the move to Córdoba. The coordinate is the corpus's Palermo Chico pin.
stops.campa: She sells the house of three floors and both cars. Nothing in the record suggests she was in debt, ill, or in any trouble; the money was good, the contracts were standing, and she was thirty-six years old. The furs and the jewellery go to friends, along with the accumulated furniture of a career, and no source reached here names a buyer for any of it or gives the month. She and her mother take the train to Córdoba and buy a small secondhand house in the hills.
suggested_refs: The 1942 liquidation: the Palermo Chico house, two automobiles, and the distributed possessions

stops.name: Salsipuedes, the modest house in the hills
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the move to Salsipuedes with her mother in 1942; no month is given and July orders the segment only. The coordinate is the Salsipuedes centroid from its own es.wikipedia article, correcting a pin about 2.5 kilometres to the southwest that the research pool carried for the same building. The etymology of the town's name is common report and is not sourced here.
stops.campa: Salsipuedes sits in the Sierras Chicas north of Córdoba, a village of stone walls and thin soil whose name reads, in Spanish, as get out if you can. The house is modest and secondhand. Her mother comes with her, as her mother has come everywhere since she was four years old. From Buenos Aires the disappearance looks like a scandal with a piece missing, and the papers will spend forty years supplying the missing piece by invention. She is thirty-six, and she will live in this house for the next thirty-nine years.
suggested_refs: The Falcón house at Salsipuedes, Córdoba province, bought secondhand in 1942

stops.name: Salsipuedes, the tercera franciscana
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests her status as a tercera franciscana, a lay tertiary of the Franciscan third order, and explicitly distinguishes this from being a professed nun; en.wikipedia calls her a 'tertiary nun', which blurs the same distinction. No date of entry into the third order is given anywhere, so this date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: She takes on the life of a tercera franciscana, a lay tertiary of the third order: a rule, a discipline, and a habit, without the vows and without the cloister. A tertiary keeps the rule while living in the world. The country decides she is a nun, because nun is the shorter word. It is not what she is, the distinction matters to her, and she does not come down out of the sierras to correct anybody who is getting it wrong in print. Eighty years on, English Wikipedia still calls her a tertiary nun.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan third order in Córdoba province; no entry record for Falcón was located in this research

stops.name: Salsipuedes, the sister who is not spoken to
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date. es.wikipedia states that after the withdrawal she had no further contact with her sister Adhelma; no year, no cause and no quarrel is recorded, and this date only places the fact inside the long retreat. What Adhelma is later accused of belongs to 1989 and is her sister's accusation, not a finding.
stops.campa: Her sister Adhelma, who also sang and never got past the provincial circuits, is cut off from the year of the withdrawal onward. There is no reconciliation, no recorded quarrel, no letter that anybody kept: only the fact of no contact, stated in one line and never explained. Amanda drops out of the account entirely. Two women share a house in the hills and the rest of the family is somewhere on the other side of the country. What Adhelma was doing in those provincial towns will surface in 1989.
suggested_refs: Adhelma Falcone and Amanda Falcone, singers, whose careers are documented nowhere reached in this research

stops.name: Salsipuedes, the death of Cornelia Boesio
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates the mother's death to 1981 and says she was over ninety; no month or day is given and the defaults are 01. The quote is one contiguous sentence from the March 1982 interview printed in Clarín on 5 January 2002 and is verbatim; it postdates this stop by roughly a year.
stops.campa: Her mother dies past ninety. They had slept in the same room since the night Ada was born: the manager who made Falcón out of Falcone, the chaperone through seventeen years of studios, the woman who got on the train to Córdoba in 1942 without a recorded word of argument. Thirty-nine years in the same small house in the hills, and the daughter is now seventy-five and alone for the first time in her life. No source reached here says where Cornelia Boesio is buried, or who came to the funeral, or whether anybody in Buenos Aires was told.
stops.quote: Desde que nací, dormí junto a mi madre, y su muerte me destrozó.
stops.quote_source: Ada Falcón, interview of March 1982, quoted in Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002
suggested_refs: Cornelia Boesio, died 1981, Córdoba province; burial place not established in this research
sources: Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002

stops.name: Córdoba province, the retreat house with no address
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia says only that after her mother's death she lodged, in her character as a Franciscan tertiary, in a casa de retiro. No town, no congregation, and no month are given. The coordinate is deliberately her last attested address at Salsipuedes rather than an invented one; the research pool pinned this to Cosquín, which no source supports, and conflated it with the later Camillian home at Molinari, which is a different institution of a different order.
stops.campa: With her mother gone she leaves the house and enters a casa de retiro as a Franciscan tertiary. Spanish Wikipedia says that much and stops: no town, no name for the order's house, no month in the year. The house at Salsipuedes stands empty. Later she will be found in a Camillian home at Molinari, some twenty kilometres west, which is a different institution of a different order and is not this one. For most of the next twenty years there is no address for Ada Falcón anywhere in the public record.
suggested_refs: The unnamed Franciscan casa de retiro of 1981, unlocated in every source reached here

stops.name: Córdoba province, the sentence with the vision in it
stops.date_confidence: the quote is verbatim from an interview of March 1982, printed in Sibila Camps's Clarín obituary of 5 January 2002 and reproduced in es.wikipedia's first reference; no day within March is given. The place of the interview is not stated and the pin is her last attested area of residence. This is the passage the secondary literature routinely truncates: two separate lenses of the research pool quoted it with the vision clause silently removed, and one of them then concluded on that basis that the vision was unattested tradition.
stops.campa: Forty years after she vanished a reporter gets her to explain it, and she does, in one sentence that has been quoted ever since and cut almost as often, because the clause people drop is the one in the middle. She had riches and beauty. She had a marvellous vision of the Lord. She did not hesitate an instant. Take the vision out and the renunciation is a mystery, which is the version that sold newspapers. Leave it in and it is a decision, and it is the only account of it she ever gave.
stops.quote: En plena juventud tuve riquezas y belleza, tuve una visión maravillosa del Señor y no vacilé un instante en dejarlo todo y recluirme en las sierras con mamita, en un convento franciscano, y vivir con humildad. Desde que nací, dormí junto a mi madre, y su muerte me destrozó.
stops.quote_source: Ada Falcón, interview of March 1982, quoted in Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002
suggested_refs: Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002, which prints the 1982 and 1989 and 1995 interview material together
sources: Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the return over the royalties
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the 1989 return, the accusation against Odeón for refusing to reissue her records, and the accusation that her sister Adhelma had toured provincial towns passing as her and signing autographs in her name; no month or day is given and the defaults are 01. The phrase 'for thirty years' comes from her own quoted words, not from the encyclopedia's summary. No case, no proof, and no counter-statement by Adhelma was located in this research.
stops.campa: She comes back to Buenos Aires at eighty-three and makes accusations. Odeón will not reissue her records. Somebody else has been collecting her rights for thirty years. Her sister Adhelma has been going round the provincial towns singing as Ada Falcón and signing autographs with her name. She will not name the powerful man behind it, saying only that he is dead and that he told her he would make her starve to death. No proof is produced and no case is brought. She goes back to Córdoba.
stops.quote: Durante treinta años cobró otra persona todos mis derechos; fue una venganza de una persona muy poderosa que ya murió, que me dijo que me iba a hacer morir de hambre.
stops.quote_source: Ada Falcón, 1989, quoted in Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002

stops.name: Molinari, the hogar San Camilo on Route 38
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia says only 'durante sus últimas décadas', during her last decades, for the Molinari residence; the 1990s dating that circulates is unsourced and this date orders the segment only. es.wikipedia's article on Molinari places the locality 4 kilometres north of the centre of Cosquín, not 5, names the congregation as Las Hijas de San Camilo, and puts their hogar de ancianos San Camilo on Ruta Nacional 38; the coordinate is that article's figure for Molinari. Wolf's remark about her reading is from the 2004 Página/12 interview and is quoted below at the filming stop.
stops.campa: Molinari is four kilometres north of Cosquín on Ruta Nacional 38: a handful of houses, a convent of the Hijas de San Camilo, and a home for old people. She moves in among strangers who are also old, in a valley that fills every January with tourists coming to the folklore festival at Cosquín, none of whom are told that the most recorded woman in the history of Argentine tango is four kilometres up the road. The sisters tell visitors she cannot read. A visitor brings her magazines and she reads them perfectly.
suggested_refs: The hogar de ancianos San Camilo, Ruta Nacional 38, Molinari, Córdoba, run by Las Hijas de San Camilo

stops.name: Molinari, the camera she lets in
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia states she had not allowed her picture to be taken for nearly sixty years and permitted the filmmakers to interview her shortly before her death; no filming date is given by any source and 2002 is impossible, since she died on 4 January of that year, so the interview is dated here to 2001 at the latest. The 'No recuerdo' answer is verbatim from Sandra Chaher's Página/12 interview with Sergio Wolf, published January 2004. Wolf's own remark about senile dementia is from the same piece.
stops.campa: Sergio Wolf and Lorena Muñoz find her and she lets them film, which she has let nobody do for nearly sixty years. She is ninety-five. Wolf asks whether Francisco Canaro had been the great love of her life and gets two words back. Whether that is refusal, exhaustion, illness, or the last exercise of a discipline she has kept since 1942, Wolf will not say either; he calls it an indiscernible zone between what memory selects at that age and what the disease takes.
stops.quote_source: Ada Falcón to Sergio Wolf, filmed interview, quoted in Sandra Chaher, 'Un misterio llamado Ada,' Página/12, January 2004

stops.name: Molinari, the death at ninety-six
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by es.wikipedia and corroborated by en.wikipedia: natural causes at ninety-six after a long arteriosclerosis, in the San Camilo home at Molinari. The epithet la emperatriz del tango is attested for her but its attribution specifically to the 2002 obituaries is not sourced. The tag-line quoted is given by Clarín as an anonymous characterisation by the graphic press; a near-identical phrase is separately attributed to Sergio Wolf in Página/12, and the discrepancy is left open.
stops.campa: On the fourth of January she dies at ninety-six in the San Camilo home, of a heart worn out under a long arteriosclerosis. She has outlived the orchestra, the label, the radio station, the man, and the century she recorded in. The obituaries call her la emperatriz del tango, the empress of tango. They also reprint the line the graphic press had coined for her decades earlier, which was true neither at twenty nor at forty: puta a los 20, monja a los 40, a whore at twenty, a nun at forty.
stops.quote: puta a los 20, monja a los 40
stops.quote_source: the Argentine graphic press, characterising Falcón's life, quoted in Sibila Camps, 'Ada Falcón fue un mito del tango,' Clarín, 5 January 2002; a near-identical phrase is attributed to Sergio Wolf in Página/12, January 2004

stops.name: Cementerio de la Chacarita, the pantheon of SADAIC
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia attests the transfer of her remains to Buenos Aires and the interment in the SADAIC pantheon at Chacarita near Canaro's plot; en.wikipedia corroborates a mausoleum for famous artists without naming SADAIC. Canaro's own presence in the pantheon is independently attested by es.wikipedia's article on him. No source gives the date of the transfer, and this date is placed the day after her death purely to order the segment. The coordinate is the cemetery figure from its own es.wikipedia article, reconciling three different pins the research pool carried for one cemetery.
stops.campa: Her body goes back to the city she left in 1942 and is laid in the pantheon of SADAIC, the authors' and composers' society, inside the great municipal cemetery at Chacarita that holds most of the tango dead of the century. Francisco Canaro is in the same pantheon, put there by the same society for the same reason, which is that they both wrote and both sang and both paid their dues. The last thing recorded about her is an approximate location inside a building full of colleagues. No source reached here gives the plot, the sector, or the date of the transfer.
suggested_refs: The Panteón de la Sociedad Argentina de Autores y Compositores, Cementerio de la Chacarita, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Salsipuedes, the house opens as La Joyita
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia's articles on Falcón and on Salsipuedes both attest the 2013 conversion of her house into a private museum named Casona & Museo La Joyita; no month or day is given and the defaults are 01. The street address and the current operating status could not be confirmed, local press coverage returning 403 and 404 errors during this research. The coordinate is the Salsipuedes centroid.
stops.campa: The house in the sierras opens as a private museum and takes the name she was given at four years old: Casona & Museo La Joyita. Furniture, photographs, dresses from the recording years, the objects of a career she sold off deliberately and which came back to her afterwards in pieces, bought and donated by other people. Visitors walk through the rooms where she spent thirty-nine years not singing. What the street address is, and whether the doors are open this year, could not be established from anything reachable.
suggested_refs: Casona & Museo La Joyita, Salsipuedes, Córdoba, opened 2013; street address unconfirmed
